overview: 2...d6 is a crossroads, not a single set-up. It is the move order that leads to the Najdorf, Dragon, Scheveningen and Classical/Richter-Rauzer after 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nc3 (s4). The open Sicilian is open and extremely complex: White has a lead in development and extra kingside space, Black has a central pawn majority and the open c-file (s1). White often castles queenside against Black's queenside counterplay, giving opposite-side attacks (Yugoslav Attack, English Attack) (s1). 2...d6 also keeps ...d5 off for a move, which is why White has quieter tries here: 3.Bc4, 3.Nc3 and 3.d3 or the Alapin-like 3.d4 cxd4 4.c3 (Tartakower, in the subtree) (s3). The root is described as combative and unbalanced (s2), but how sharp a game is depends heavily on whether White plays 3.d4 or an anti-Sicilian.

white_ideas.idea: Open Sicilian: 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 and use the development lead and kingside space
English Attack against the Najdorf: Be3, f3, Qd2, 0-0-0 and g4
Richter-Rauzer 6.Bg5 against the Classical, threatening to double Black's pawns with Bxf6
Yugoslav Attack against the Dragon: opposite-side castling and a kingside attack
Anti-Sicilian 3.Bc4: stops ...d5 for a move; the bishop can become a target to ...a6/...b5 or ...e6/...d5, so White spends tempi on Bb3 or a3

black_ideas.idea: Counterplay down the open c-file and on the queenside with the central pawn majority
Small centre with pawns on d6 and e6: a solid barrier, control of d5 and e5, flexible ...e5 or ...d5 later
Break with ...d5 (or ...b5 in the Scheveningen) to free the position
Najdorf ...a6 to prepare ...e5 and stop Bb5+; Dragon fianchetto and a race on opposite wings
Against 3.Bc4, play ...Nf6, ...e6 and ...d5 for a comfortable game

typical_structures.structure: Open Sicilian: White d4 pawn gone, Black d6/e-pawn centre, half-open c-file for Black and d-file for White
Scheveningen small centre (d6 and e6 pawns), Black waiting to break with ...d5

character.notes: Chess.com calls the Sicilian combative and a source of dynamic, sharp, unbalanced positions (s2). The open Sicilian is described as open and extremely complex, with a race between attack and counterattack in the Dragon (s1). The root as a whole leans Sharp, because 3.d4 lines (Najdorf, Dragon, Richter-Rauzer, English Attack) dominate the subtree. The anti-Sicilian branches (3.Bc4, 3.Nc3, 3.d3, c3) are calmer and a few are comfortable for Black (s3). The most-played subtree lines in the input are all 3.d4 Open lines, the next most are 3.Bc4 and 3.Nc3.

gambit.notes: No material is given in the main lines. (Smith-Morra style gambits come after 2...cxd4, not 2...d6.)

soundness.notes: Fully sound: Najdorf, Dragon, Scheveningen are mainstream at top level. No source suggests anything dubious about the root. Several of White's anti-Sicilians are not threatening, e.g. 3.Bc4 loses time to retreats and Black is comfortable (s3).

structure.notes: Typical middlegame: c-pawn traded for d-pawn, so White has e4 against Black's d6 with a half-open c-file for Black. The centre is partly open, with a half-open c-file for Black and d-file for White (s1). Black keeps a pawn majority in the centre (s1). Semi-open fits the Najdorf and Dragon anchors in the taxonomy. The 3.d3 and 3.Nc3 lines are calmer and can be closed Sicilian type set-ups.

approach.notes: Not a system: a family of replies to 1.e4, played at every level including by world-class players through the Najdorf and Dragon. Standard.

level.notes: Chess.com lists the amount of theory as a drawback (s2). The open lines need a lot of memorised theory (English Attack, Richter-Rauzer, Yugoslav) and understanding of the c-file and ...d5 break. Black is the side that studies it. Dragon and Najdorf are the usual Advanced anchors; the anti-Sicilians against 2...d6 are easier. The root is therefore best read as Advanced, from Black's side.

sublines_that_differ.name: Najdorf Variation
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 a6
sublines_that_differ.how: Very sharp, theory-heavy; its own root already

sublines_that_differ.name: Dragon Variation
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 g6
sublines_that_differ.how: Opposite-side castling race (Yugoslav Attack); extremely sharp

sublines_that_differ.name: Scheveningen Variation
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 e6
sublines_that_differ.how: Small centre; more compact and flexible, still tactical

sublines_that_differ.name: Classical / Richter-Rauzer
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 Nc6 6. Bg5
sublines_that_differ.how: Pressure on Nf6; sharper if Black castles queenside

sublines_that_differ.name: 3.Nc3 / Closed-type
sublines_that_differ.how: Anti-Sicilian that can avoid the open Sicilian (own understanding, unsourced)

sublines_that_differ.name: 3.d3
sublines_that_differ.how: Slow King's Indian Attack style set-up; low theory, not sharp (own understanding, unsourced)

sublines_that_differ.name: Tartakower / Alapin-type
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 cxd4 4. c3
sublines_that_differ.how: Pawn gambit-like offer that White can often regain; quieter than the Najdorf (own understanding, unsourced)

description.claim: 2...d6 is one of the most popular and combative responses to 1.e4
description.note: The Sicilian is described as combative; 2...d6 is the most common move order into the main open lines.

description.claim: It is a gateway to the Najdorf and Dragon
Black challenges White's central control, creating an imbalanced and dynamic struggle
Perfect for ambitious, well-prepared players who thrive in sharp, double-edged battles
description.note: Theory load and sharp lines bear this out. The quieter anti-Sicilian branches are not captured.

common_plans.claim: White: seize space with early d4 and launch a kingside attack (f4-f5, g4-g5), especially with opposite-side castling
common_plans.note: English Attack uses g4; Yugoslav uses a kingside attack against opposite castling. f4-f5 fits 6.Be2 / Scheveningen lines (own understanding).

common_plans.claim: Black: counterplay on the semi-open c-file, pressure on e4, and queenside expansion with ...a6 and ...b5
common_plans.note: c-file and queenside expansion confirmed; ...a6/...b5 is the Najdorf pattern. Pressure on e4 is plausible but not directly sourced.

common_plans.claim: Black: prepare and execute the liberating ...d5 break to challenge White's centre
common_plans.note: ...d5 is the central freeing break in the small-centre set-ups.

common_plans.claim: White: control the critical d5 square to prevent Black's central break and use it as an outpost
common_plans.note: Bc4 and Nc3 aim at d5/stopping ...d5 and the small centre controls d5, so the fight is for it.
